title: Stages of life
hookLine: Hindu tradition names four stages of life, from student to renunciant

lines: A STUDENT, A PARENT, A RETIREE.
cards: A student cramming for exams wants to know why nobody will let her just get on with her life. A parent can't remember the last time the house was quiet.

A man, newly retired, stands in the kitchen at ten in the morning and has no idea what he's for. Each of them is asking the same question at a different hour: what is this part of my life supposed to be about?
Hindu tradition has an old answer. Not one rule for a whole life, but four. Today's word: ashrama.

teach.b: First, the four. In Hindu tradition, the ashramas are stages of life. In the student stage, brahmacharya, a young person learns from a teacher.
In the householder stage, grihastha, a person marries, works, raises a family and keeps a home. In the forest stage, vanaprastha, the forest dweller steps back from the busy middle of life.
And in sannyasa, the renunciant lets go of home and possessions altogether. Second, the hinge. The Laws of Manu, an old Hindu law book, gives a picture of when to move on.
In paraphrase: when a householder sees his skin wrinkled, his hair white, and the sons of his sons, he may go to the forest. Not a birthday. The sign is that the next generation has arrived.
Third, the householder's honor. It's easy to hear the stages as a ladder, with the renunciant at the top and the busy parent at the bottom. Manu says something different about the middle.
As all creatures live by the air, the other stages live by the householder's support. The student is fed, the wanderer is given alms, because someone is working and keeping a home.
In this picture, work isn't a detour from the spiritual life. For a season, it is the spiritual life.
Fourth, a map, not a cage.
The old texts were written for men of particular classes, and Hindus read and live the stages in different ways today, some as a strict pattern, some as a loose map.
What the map offers anyone is a question: not what is life for, but what is this stage for?

how: Hindus who follow the ashrama pattern treat each stage as having its own duties: study for the student, work and family for the householder, a gradual stepping back for the forest dweller, and renunciation for those who take sannyasa.

o: a prayer said at sunrise to greet the new day
a fast kept for one week before a festival
a stage of life in Hindu tradition, with its own work

games.q: the four stages — tap the pairs.

s: in Manu, the sign to move on is a fixed birthday
the picture is wrinkled skin, white hair, and the sons of one's sons.
Manu compares the householder to the air that all creatures live by
the other stages live by the householder's support.
all Hindus treat the stages as one strict rule
Hindus read and live them in different ways; some as a pattern, some as a loose map.

games.q: you're a householder. by Manu's picture, what tells you it's time to step back to the forest?
o: the first time you feel tired.
games.why: Manu's sign is the next generation arriving: wrinkled skin, white hair, and the sons of one's sons.

practice: Hear the four names again, student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, and without judging, ask which one describes this season of your life; maybe more than one. Name your stage quietly to yourself.
Then ask what this stage asks of you, not forever, just now, and stay with the first plain answer.

wordCard.voice: Ashrama. A stage of life in Hindu tradition: student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, each with its own work. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a stage of life in Hindu tradition; there are four.

carryVoice: Your line: my stage. Each season of a life has its own work. See you tomorrow.
